title: Stop logging inside signal handlers

cast.name: Jo
cast.role: Junior Linux service author who wants a helpful shutdown log

cast.name: Ren
cast.role: Systems engineer who keeps asynchronous handlers tiny

glossary.note: A request that a process terminate cleanly.

glossary.full: Safe to call asynchronously from a signal handler
glossary.note: The function is safe if a signal interrupts ordinary code while it is running.

glossary.full: Linux file descriptor for receiving signals
glossary.note: Blocked signals can be read in the normal event loop.

key_points: A signal can interrupt code while stdio or allocator state is halfway through an operation.
A handler should only use async-signal-safe operations and minimal shared state.
On Linux, blocked signals can be consumed through signalfd in the ordinary event loop.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A fictional Linux worker receives a shutdown request mid-job. Jo adds a friendly log inside the signal callback.

beats.speaker: rookie
beats.text: When SIGTERM arrives, I call printf to explain why the worker stopped. The handler is tiny; what could go wrong?

beats.speaker: senior
beats.text: The signal can interrupt printf while its shared buffer is half updated. Calling it again may corrupt output. Many library routines have this problem.

visuals.text: printf can re-enter a half-updated buffer

beats.speaker: rookie
beats.text: Which operation is safe there? Can I allocate a message for later?

beats.speaker: senior
beats.text: No allocation or formatted logging. Use async-signal-safe functions and minimal state. In a single-threaded program, a handler can set a volatile signal-atomic flag; ordinary code cleans up.

beats.speaker: rookie
beats.text: Our Linux service waits on file descriptors. Can signals join that event loop instead of interrupting arbitrary work?

beats.speaker: senior
beats.text: Yes. Block chosen signals before starting worker threads, create signalfd, then read records in the normal loop. Ordinary code can log and clean up; this interface is Linux-specific.

beats.speaker: rookie
beats.text: So sigaction installs a tiny fallback, while signalfd fits Linux event loops. Neither handler should call printf, malloc, or unsafe library code.

beats.speaker: senior
beats.text: Keep asynchronous work tiny; let ordinary code report and clean up. Shutdown stays clear if SIGTERM arrives awkwardly.

expect.text: printf can re-enter a half-updated buffer
expect.note: The main reveal explains why formatted I/O is unsafe in the handler.
